title: Arbitrary base change of semistable marked curves and fibrewise stability
statement: Let $T$ be any scheme. First, for every multipointed $T$-curve $(X,D)$ (not necessarily semistable) and every morphism $T'\to T$, the pair $(X\times_TT',D\times_TT')$ is a multipointed $T'$-curve; if moreover $T$ and $T'$ are integral [def-pc-integral-scheme] and $T'\to T$ maps the generic point [def-sc-generic-point] of $T'$ to that of $T$, and the generic curve of $X$ is smooth and its generic marking is etale, then the same holds for the pulled-back pair. Now let $(Y,E)$ be a semistable multipointed $T$-curve. For every morphism $T'\to T$, the pair $(Y\times_T T',E\times_T T')$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is again a semistable multipointed $T'$-curve: both structural morphisms are flat and finitely presented of pure relative dimensions $1$ and $0$, the marking is a closed immersion and etale over $T'$, the curve has only ordinary nodes in geometric fibres, and the marking lies in the relative smooth locus. The relative smooth locus pulls back to the relative smooth locus. These properties are local for an open cover of $T$. More generally, for a compatible morphism of multipointed pairs $f:(Y,E)\to(X,D)$ with semistable source, the condition that every geometric fibre of $Y$ has no irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$ that is contracted by $f$ and meets the marking and singular locus in at most two points is preserved by arbitrary base change and is local for open covers of $T$. This assertion concerns the geometric stability condition; it does not assert that an arbitrary base change of an $\eta$-modification is still a modification. A multipointed curve $(X,D)$ over a scheme $T$ means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] morphisms $X\to T$, $D\to T$ of pure relative dimensions $1$, $0$ and a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow X$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; $D$ may be empty and $X$ need not be separated or proper over $T$. It is semistable if every singular point of every geometric fibre has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ over its algebraically closed residue field, $D\to T$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism], and $D$ lies in the relative smooth locus [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Geometric fibres are [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]; the local completion is at the maximal ideal [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], and $\Omega[[u,v]]$ denotes the two-variable formal power series ring [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series].

source.place: Stacks Tags 0C59 (curves.tex, lemma-nodal-family), 0C5B (lemma-base-change-nodal-family), and the usual base-change theorems for flatness, finite presentation, closed immersions, etaleness and smoothness; Temkin §1.2, pp. 2--3 (semistability and exceptional components defined on geometric fibres); ILO X Theorem 3.4 Step 4, pp. 160--161.

proof.text: For both structural maps, [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change], [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](3) and [lem-trf-relative-dimension-base-change] preserve flatness, finite presentation and pure fibre dimensions $1,0$. The induced marking is the base change of the old closed immersion, hence closed by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]. This gives multipointedness. Under the generic-point condition the new generic fibres are scalar extensions along $\kappa(\eta_T)\to\kappa(\eta_{T\prime})$; [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2) and [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change] preserve smoothness and etaleness.

source.place: Tags 0C59, 0C5B and 0CBY; assembly of the five extracted arguments.

proof.text: For $Y\to T$, semistability and Step 1 give the hypotheses of [lem-trf-chosen-nodal-fibres-universal]: flat, locally finitely presented, nonempty fibres pure of dimension $1$, and nodes on the chosen-closure geometric fibres. It shows that for every algebraically closed field $\Omega$ and every $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ each nonsmooth point of $Y_\Omega$ has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$, and that the relative smooth locus $U$ of $Y\to T$ satisfies $U\prime=U\times_TT\prime$. For $t\prime\in T\prime$ with chosen closure $\Omega$ of $\kappa(t\prime)$, associating fibre products [def-pc-fibre-product] identifies $Y\prime\times_{T\prime}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ over $\Omega$ with $Y\times_T\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ for the composite $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T\prime\to T$, so every nonsmooth point of every geometric fibre of $Y\prime$ is an ordinary node. The structural properties come from Step 1; [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change] preserves the marking's etaleness, and $E\subset U$ gives $E\prime=E\times_TT\prime\subset U\times_TT\prime=U\prime$.

source.place: Tags 0C59, 0C5B and 0CBY; assembly of the five extracted arguments.

proof.text: For algebraically closed $k\subset L$, [lem-trf-geometric-components-projective-line-descent] identifies the reduced components and preserves and reflects being $\mathbf P^1$. [lem-trf-nodal-marking-special-point-incidence] preserves each component's number of distinct marked or singular points, and [lem-trf-projective-line-contraction-scalar-extension] preserves and reflects contraction. Thus no forbidden component can appear after extension. For $t\prime\mapsto t$, embed the chosen closure of $\kappa(t)$ into that of $\kappa(t\prime)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-extension-embeds-algebraically-closed]; associating fibre products [def-pc-fibre-product] identifies the new fibre morphism with that scalar extension. This proves geometric stability under arbitrary base change.

source.place: Tags 0C59, 0C5B and 0CBY; assembly of the five extracted arguments.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-structural-fibrewise-open-locality] to the structural maps, marking and fibre morphism. Use its geometric-diagram predicate first for nodality and then for absence of the forbidden contracted component. Its smooth-locus clause checks the marking inclusion. These equivalences give all asserted open-cover locality statements. They do not assert preservation of modifications.
